claims.text: The starting catalyst is a near-equiatomic multi-principal-element automotive alloy containing Cu, Ni, and minimal platinum-group metals.
The elements in the initial catalyst are homogeneously distributed.
Mild thermal oxidation/reduction cycling will drive selective Cu segregation to the catalyst surface.
The treatment will enrich the catalyst surface in Cu without increasing platinum-group-metal content.
Surface-enriched Cu will form active Cu–O species.
Cu surface enrichment will alter surface adsorption sites.
The Cu-enriched surface will provide lower-activation-energy pathways for CO oxidation.
The Cu-enriched surface will provide lower-activation-energy pathways for hydrocarbon oxidation.
Cu-induced changes in adsorption will improve resistance to H2O poisoning.
Cu-induced changes in adsorption will improve resistance to NO poisoning.
The Cu-rich surface layer will promote self-healing or slower degradation during thermal cycling and mileage-related stress.
The pretreatment will lower CO and hydrocarbon light-off temperature relative to the unmodified catalyst.
The treated catalyst is expected to achieve low-temperature oxidation below 150 °C.
The treated catalyst will maintain better activity in the presence of H2O and NO than the unmodified catalyst.
The treated catalyst will degrade more slowly during long-term accelerated aging than the unmodified catalyst.
The proposed benefits should persist under transient, low-temperature exhaust containing H2O and NO and under accelerated aging representative of vehicle-lifetime mileage.
Outside the specified exhaust and aging conditions, the benefits and durability of the Cu-rich surface may be less pronounced.
